news.2026-10-29-cuba-onu-embargo-vote.ti: The UN condemns the US embargo on Cuba once again, but Cuba loses 35 votes in a year
news.2026-10-29-cuba-onu-embargo-vote.su: On 28 October the General Assembly voted 130 against the embargo, 17 for keeping it and 25 abstentions. Last year, 165 countries backed Cuba.
news.2026-10-29-cuba-onu-embargo-vote.po: On 28 October, the UN General Assembly called for an end to the US embargo on Cuba by 130 votes to 17, with 25 abstentions, for the 34th year in a row [1][2][3].

In 2025 the vote was 165 in favour, 7 against and 12 abstentions: Cuba therefore loses 35 votes of support in a year [1][2]. The United States, Israel, Ukraine, Argentina and the United Arab Emirates are among the 17 countries that voted against [1].

The day before, the debate was tense: Cuba's foreign minister, Bruno Rodríguez, interrupted US ambassador Mike Waltz, and the session was briefly suspended [1]. Washington argues that Cuba's crisis comes from its own government, not from the embargo [1].
news.2026-10-29-cuba-onu-embargo-vote.wh: Key point: the text binds no one, but each year it measures how many countries are still willing to oppose Washington in public [1][2].

This time, Washington points to the rise in abstentions to say that its pressure to isolate Cuba is starting to pay off [1]. The resolution also cites the 1996 US Helms-Burton Act and asks the UN Secretary-General for a report at the next session [1].
news.2026-10-29-cuba-onu-embargo-vote.fo: The vote changes nothing in your daily life right now: above all, it shows where the diplomatic balance of power around Cuba stands [1][2].

news.2026-10-29-colombie-amazonie-reserv: Colombia strips the Amazon of its protection from mining and oil
The Environment Ministry has revoked the reserve created in August, which covered about 42% of the country. Opponents see a green light for extractive industries.
Colombia's Environment Ministry has revoked Resolution 0961 of 2026, which made the Amazon a "definitive" reserve closed to new mining concessions and new oil contracts [1][2].

The area covered about 483,283 km², roughly 42% of the country's mainland territory [1]. The ministry explains that the text was adopted without completing prior consultation with Black, Afro-Colombian, Raizal and Palenquero communities [1].

Revoking it does not mean everything is allowed: projects must still comply with other rules, such as the 1959 forest reserve law or the national parks system [1]. Former minister Irene Vélez, who defended the text, criticises the decision and points to an interest in rare earths, which remains her accusation, not an established fact [2][3].
Key point: the protection of the Colombian Amazon rested on a single text, signed at the end of Gustavo Petro's term, and a new government was able to undo it within a few weeks [1][3].

Environment Minister Fabio Arjona argues there was a procedural flaw, while his opponents speak of a setback for the forest [3]. The issue will turn on the rules that remain in force and on possible court challenges [1].
Nothing changes in the short term for you: the decision simply opens the possibility of new mining and oil projects in an area that was closed until now [1].

news.2026-10-29-irak-syrie-visite-oleodu: An Iraqi prime minister in Damascus for the first time since Assad's fall, with oil at the top of the agenda
Ali al-Zaidi met Syrian president Ahmed al-Sharaa on 28 October. The Iraqi prime minister's office talks of exporting oil through the Baniyas pipeline, up to 2 million barrels a day.

On 28 October, Iraqi prime minister Ali al-Zaidi was welcomed at Damascus airport by Syrian president Ahmed al-Sharaa [1][2]. According to one source, it is the first visit by an Iraqi head of government since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 [2].

The Iraqi prime minister's office says it discussed exporting Iraqi oil through the Baniyas pipeline, which could carry up to 2 million barrels a day, as well as trade, agriculture and border security [1].
No signed agreement was reported [1]. For their part, the authorities of Iraqi Kurdistan protested against agreements made by Baghdad without consulting them [4].
Key point: the war has disrupted Iraq's oil exports; in June, it had already begun sending a little through Syria [3].
For Syria, becoming the corridor for Iraqi black gold would be a way to regain an economic role; al-Sharaa stressed how important this role as a trade route is for Iraq [1][2].
An oil route that bypasses the Gulf can help supply the market while the war disrupts exports, but this one still exists only on paper [1][3].

news.2026-10-29-azerbaidjan-turquie-voil: The headscarf at school strains Baku–Ankara ties: Erdogan fires an adviser, Azerbaijan bans 31 Turks from entering
A school uniform rule, enforced since 12 October, has set off protests in Azerbaijan and then an open dispute with Turkey.

On 21 September, Baku adopted uniform rules that ban pupils and teachers in public schools from wearing clothes contrary to secularism, without mentioning the headscarf [1][2]. Since about 12 October, veiled pupils and teachers have been refused entry to schools [1].
The Interior Ministry says it has arrested 37 people for disturbing public order; Amnesty, for its part, reports arrests of peaceful protesters [1][2][4].

Oktay Saral, an adviser to the Turkish president, called on X for Azerbaijan to reverse this "mistake"; Recep Tayyip Erdogan then fired him [3]. Baku also banned 31 Turks from entering the country, politicians and public figures who had criticised the rule, and Ilham Aliyev warned that nobody should "interfere with our way of life" [3][5].
Key point: a domestic issue, school, has taken on a diplomatic dimension between Baku and Ankara [3][5].
The ruling party in Baku rejects any interference and defends rules that, it says, are based on equality and secularism [4]. NGOs, for their part, speak of a violation of the right to education [4].
Nothing changes in your daily life, but the episode shows that a simple school rule can be enough to ruffle two neighbouring governments [3][5].

news.2026-10-29-gabon-reseaux-sociaux-ro: Gabon reopens social media after eight months, but you will have to show ID
The suspension, imposed on 17 February, had been criticised by the opposition, young people and businesses. Many Gabonese got around it with VPNs.

The communications regulator (HAC) announced on Saturday that the suspension of social media, in place since 17 February, is being lifted; officially it had been imposed because online content was fuelling tensions [1][2].
It explains its decision by talks with the major tech companies about moderating the platforms [2].

Reopening comes with a condition: users will have to provide official ID to sign up, which effectively ends online anonymity [2]. During the shutdown, many used VPNs, and the opposition denounced an abuse of power [2][3].
Key point: the shutdown lasted eight months and was criticised by young people and businesses [3].
Requiring ID to use these platforms is a way of reducing anonymity, which worries defenders of freedoms [2].
When a country cuts the networks, its people and businesses feel it quickly: it is a risk worth knowing about before working with it [3].
news.2026-10-29-nepal-fonds-pertes-domma: After the floods, the UN climate fund sets aside its first $20 million for Nepal, against $4.7 billion of needs
This is the first time the "loss and damage" fund has set aside money for a country. Nepal still has to submit a project before it receives anything.
On 22 October, the board of the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage set aside $20 million for Nepal, after the deadly floods in August [1][2].
It is the fund's first payout to any country [2][3]. The Nepali government estimates reconstruction at about $4.7 billion, which puts these $20 million below 1% of the needs [1][2].
The money is not yet released: Nepal must first submit a project proposal [1]. The floods killed more than 1,400 people, according to sources, with tolls varying around 1,500 [2].
Key point: this is the first test of a fund created to help countries hit by climate damage, and the gap with the needs is huge [2][3].
Campaigners and experts consider the sum far too small and say rich countries responded coldly to Nepal's request [2].
This debate over who pays for climate damage comes back at every major climate summit; here, the aid covers less than 1% of the estimated needs [1][2].

news.2026-10-29-singapour-indonesie-brum: Singapore and Indonesia will follow the money of the companies behind the toxic haze
The two foreign ministers announced on 27 October a joint team to prosecute the companies linked to forest fires.
On 27 October, in Jakarta, Singapore and Indonesia decided to create a joint team to pursue the companies linked to the forest fires that cause the toxic haze [1].
It is to share information, trace financial flows, gather evidence on both sides of the border and, where possible, recover assets, Indonesian minister Arrmanatha Nasir explained [1].

Singapore has already sent preventive-measures notices to 10 companies linked to the fires in Indonesia and asked 10 companies based in Singapore for information; its minister Vivian Balakrishnan promises to use "every single legal power" against those responsible, including in Singapore [1]. Bloomberg also sees it as a way to calm tensions, after an unexpected gas supply cut [2].
Key point: instead of blaming the neighbouring state, the two governments are targeting the companies and their money, which is harder to ignore [1].
This haze episode is one of the most severe in the region in more than ten years [1].
Haze does not stop at borders: that is why the two countries want to go after companies rather than trade blame [1].

news.2026-10-29-afrique-pib-reevalue-gui: The IMF raises sub-Saharan Africa's growth to 4.5%; Ethiopia and Guinea among the fastest
In its October outlook, the IMF raises its forecast for the region by 0.2 points, despite the oil shock of the Iran war.
The IMF expects 4.5% growth in sub-Saharan Africa in 2026, 0.2 points more than in its April forecasts [1].
Ethiopia, Guinea and Benin are among the fastest-growing economies, according to the report [1].
Comparing the IMF's April and October data, the Nigerian daily BusinessDay calculates that the estimated GDP of all African economies was revised up by about $99 billion [2].
Key point: higher oil prices help exporting countries, but the IMF warns that importers are under more pressure [2].
These revisions change the stated size of economies; on their own, they do not say whether people live better [2].
Growth of 4.5% is still fast compared with Europe: sub-Saharan Africa is one of the fastest-growing regions [1].
